name: Services Directive
evidence_rating: moderate: difference-in-differences and gravity studies of services trade comparing covered and uncovered services, with mixed results; a firm-level productivity study; Commission model-based estimates
summary: The Directive required Member States to remove unjustified barriers to establishing and providing services and to set up points of single contact. Studies that compare services covered by the Directive with others find that intra-EU trade in the targeted services rose by 29 to 67% (Kern, Paetzold and Winner 2021), though an earlier study finds trade was reallocated between countries rather than raised overall (Dettmer 2014), and a firm-level study finds productivity gains its author does not treat as firmly causal.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below

literature.citation: Monteagudo, J., Rutkowski, A. and Lorenzani, D. (2012), The economic impact of the Services Directive: a first assessment following implementation, European Economy Economic Papers 456, European Commission (DG ECFIN)
literature.authors: Monteagudo, J., Rutkowski, A. and Lorenzani, D.
literature.title: The economic impact of the Services Directive: a first assessment following implementation
literature.venue: European Economy Economic Papers 456, European Commission (DG ECFIN)
literature.method: quantitative assessment (barrier indicators before and after implementation, gravity-model estimates)
literature.headline: Estimates gains in intra-EU services trade, FDI and GDP from the barriers removed by implementation; authors describe it as an updated prediction rather than an assessment of full effects
literature.summary_plain: Commission economists estimated that the barriers removed by the Directive raise trade and investment in services, but stressed that this is an estimate, not a measurement of what happened.

literature.citation: National Board of Trade Sweden (Kommerskollegium) (2015), Economic effects of the European Single Market: review of the empirical literature, National Board of Trade report
literature.title: Economic effects of the European Single Market: review of the empirical literature
literature.headline: No ex-post analysis of the effects of the Services Directive available at the time of the review
literature.summary_plain: A Swedish government review of the evidence found no study that had measured the Directive's actual effects.

literature.citation: Kern, M.; Paetzold, J.; Winner, H. (2021), Cutting red tape for trade in services, The World Economy 44(10):2858-2886
literature.authors: Kern, M.; Paetzold, J.; Winner, H.
literature.title: Cutting red tape for trade in services
literature.method: triple-difference structural gravity model (PPML, multiple fixed effects), targeted vs non-targeted services, intra-EU vs other flows
literature.outcomes: bilateral services trade; domestic trade diversion; welfare
literature.headline: The Directive increased intra-EU trade in targeted services by between 29% (lower bound) and 67% (upper bound). That implies welfare gains of 0.39%-1.32% for Member States, with some diversion away from domestic flows and large differences across countries and sectors.
literature.summary_plain: Cutting paperwork for cross-border service providers substantially increased trade in the services covered by the Directive.
literature.period_geography: EU Member States vs non-EU comparators, pre/post 2009 transposition

literature.citation: Dettmer, B. (2014), Trade Effects of the European Union's Service Directive: Contrasting ex ante Estimates with Empirical Evidence, The World Economy 38(3):445-478
literature.title: Trade Effects of the European Union's Service Directive: Contrasting ex ante Estimates with Empirical Evidence
literature.method: difference-in-differences(-in-differences) gravity estimates, EU vs non-EU country pairs, 2004-2010, controlling for non-tariff barriers and RTA endogeneity
literature.headline: The Directive 'adds to a reallocation of business services trade within the EU'. It deepened new Member States' integration and raised third-country exports to the EU, while trade among the EU-10 fell and EU-15/EU-15 trade was not significantly affected.
literature.summary_plain: An early ex-post check finds the Directive mostly reshuffled who trades services with whom inside the EU rather than raising trade everywhere.

literature.citation: Olbrecht, V. (2018), Empirical Evidence of the Introduction of the Services Directive on Microeconomic Productivity, JCMS: Journal of Common Market Studies 56(6):1411-1428
literature.title: Empirical Evidence of the Introduction of the Services Directive on Microeconomic Productivity
literature.venue: JCMS: Journal of Common Market Studies 56(6):1411-1428
literature.method: difference-in-difference-in-differences on firm-level data (retail and wholesale), two control groups
literature.headline: The Directive 'significantly increased the productivity' of affected retail and wholesale firms, though the author cautions the results 'cannot be labelled as profoundly causal'.
literature.summary_plain: Shops and wholesalers covered by the Directive became more productive, though the author is careful not to claim firm proof.
literature.quality: quasi-causal (DDD), author flags identification limits; peer-reviewed
